clues.text: The house of Israel named this bread, white like coriander seed and tasting like wafers with honey.
Moses told Aaron to fill a jar with an omer of it and place it before the LORD.
The day after Israel ate the produce of Canaan, this food from God stopped for good.
When the dew fell on the Israelite camp at night, this food fell along with it.
Their appetite gone in the wilderness, the Israelites grumbled that there was nothing to see but this.
The Spirit tells the churches the one who overcomes will receive this, hidden, plus a white stone.
Jesus told the crowd that their fathers ate this in the wilderness, yet they still died.
In a wilderness cave near the Rocks of the Wild Goats, he quietly cut off a corner of King Saul's robe.
Wearing a linen ephod, he danced with all his might before the LORD as the ark was brought up.
When he heard that Nabal was dead, he sent word to Abigail asking her to become his wife.
Three mighty men risked their lives to bring him water, but he refused to drink it, calling it their blood.
To stop a plague, he paid Araunah fifty shekels of silver for a threshing floor and oxen.
Mephibosheth, the lame grandson of Saul, ate at this king's table like one of the king's own sons.
The prophet Nathan told this king, "You are that man!" and reminded him that God had anointed him over Israel.
In Pharaoh's dream, seven sickly, thin cows came up out of it and stood on its bank.
Pharaoh commanded his people to throw every son born to the Hebrews into it.
Moses' mother put her baby in a papyrus basket coated with tar and set it among the reeds along its bank.
Before Pharaoh and his officials, Aaron raised the staff and struck its water, and it all turned to blood.
Moses warned Pharaoh that it would teem with frogs that would come into his palace and onto his bed.
Through Ezekiel, God spoke against the king of Egypt, who boasted that he had made it himself.
In a prophecy about Egypt, Isaiah said the fishermen who cast hooks into it would mourn.
In Egypt, God told Israel to eat this meal in haste, dressed for travel with sandals on and staff in hand.
When Israelite children asked about this sacrifice, they were to hear that the LORD spared their homes in Egypt.
Moses was told that an Israelite unclean from a dead body, or away on a journey, could still keep this.
Camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho, the Israelites kept this on the evening of the fourteenth day.
King Hezekiah sent letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, inviting them to Jerusalem to keep this feast of the LORD.
King Josiah gave 30,000 lambs and goats and 3,000 bulls from his own flocks and herds for these offerings.
Pilate reminded the Jews of their custom that he release one prisoner to them at this feast.
A servant girl in the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where many had gathered to pray.
When Peter knocked at the outer gate of Mary's house, this servant girl came to answer it.
At the gate of Mary's house, this servant girl recognized Peter just by hearing his voice.
So overjoyed to hear Peter outside, this servant girl forgot to open the gate for him.
Leaving Peter outside, this servant girl ran in and announced, "Peter is standing at the gate!"
Believers praying in Mary's house told this servant girl she was out of her mind about Peter.
When this servant girl kept insisting Peter was at the gate, the believers said it must be his angel.
The wife of Phinehas, Eli's daughter-in-law, went into labor and bore him when she heard the ark was captured.
As his mother lay dying in Eli's family, the women with her said not to fear, for she had borne a son.
He was born after news came that the ark was taken, the same news that made his grandfather Eli fall and die.
His mother named him, saying the glory had departed from Israel because the ark of God was captured.
When the Philistines took the ark of God, his father died in that battle alongside his uncle Hophni.
He was a grandson of Eli, the priest of the LORD in Shiloh, through Eli's son Phinehas.
While Jonathan secretly left Saul's camp, this man's nephew Ahijah was there wearing an ephod.
Jesus carried His own cross out to this place, which has a Hebrew name.
Soldiers brought Jesus here after making Simon of Cyrene carry His cross.
Here Jesus was offered wine mixed with gall, but after tasting it He refused to drink.
At this place Jesus was crucified between two others, one on each side of Him.
Here soldiers divided the garments of Jesus by casting lots, then sat down to keep watch over Him.
Many Jews read Pilate's sign over Jesus, because this place of crucifixion was near the city.
Near the spot where Jesus was crucified was a garden holding a new tomb.
God told a man to make it of gopher wood, with rooms, and coat it with pitch inside and out.
God set its size at three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
God said to give it a roof, a door in its side, and lower, middle, and upper decks.
For forty days the waters rose on the earth and lifted it high above the ground.
On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, it came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
A dove found no place to rest her foot, so she returned, and a hand reached out to bring her back inside it.
By faith a man warned about things not yet seen built it in godly fear to save his family.
In Ezekiel's prophecy, this land and Dedan ask an invader if he has come to seize plunder.
Praying for the king, a psalmist asks that the kings of this land and Seba offer gifts.
Job says the travelers of this place hope to find water, like the caravans of Tema.
A psalm praying for the king asks that gold from this land be given to him.
Isaiah foresees camels from Midian and Ephah, and all from this land bringing gold and frankincense.
Through Jeremiah, God asks what use frankincense from this land is when Israel's sacrifices do not please Him.
In Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, merchants of this land and Raamah traded gold, spices, and precious stones.
Near a field full of these, the Philistines banded together and Israel's troops fled from them.
Beds, basins and earthen vessels were brought to David, along with flour, beans and these.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi, Machir and Barzillai brought him these along with wheat and barley.
David's hungry, weary people in the wilderness were given these, with roasted grain, honey, curds and cheese.
Shammah the Hararite took his stand against the Philistines in a field full of these.
God told Ezekiel to put these in one container with wheat, millet and spelt to make bread.
God told Ezekiel to eat bread made partly from these during the 390 days he lay on his side.

accepted: Hosanna to the Son of David

clues.text: As Jesus rode into Jerusalem, crowds ahead of Him and behind Him shouted this twice, along with a blessing.
Children shouted this in the temple courts, and the chief priests and scribes grew indignant.
On the road into Jerusalem, people blessed the coming kingdom of their father David, then cried this.
People carried branches out to meet Jesus, and this single word came first in their shouting.
Those walking ahead of Jesus and those following behind Him all shouted this one word.
A massive crowd spread cloaks and tree branches on the road for Jesus, then shouted this to Him.
A large crowd at the feast heard Jesus was coming to Jerusalem and went out to meet Him shouting this.
After coming up from Egypt with Abram, this man also had flocks and herds and tents of his own.
Parting company with Abram, he chose the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and set out east.
Raiding kings carried this man off with all his possessions, since he was living in Sodom.
Two angels arrived at Sodom in the evening and found him sitting in the city gateway.
In Sodom, his sons-in-law thought he was joking when he warned that the LORD would destroy the city.
Afraid to stay in Zoar, he and his two daughters went to live in a cave in the mountains.
Peter calls him a righteous man whom God rescued while he was distressed by the conduct of the lawless.
John, a partner in tribulation with his fellow believers, was here because of the word of God.
In this place, on the Lord's day, a man in the Spirit heard a loud voice like a trumpet behind him.
In this place, a voice told a man to write on a scroll what he saw and send it to seven churches.
In this place, a man turned to see the voice speaking with him and saw seven golden lampstands.
In this place, a man saw One like the Son of Man holding seven stars in His right hand.
In this place, a man fell like a dead man at the feet of One who told him not to be afraid.
The writer greeting seven churches in the province of Asia says he was on this island.
Speaking to Job, God pointed to a creature He made along with Job that feeds on grass like an ox.
God told Job to see the strength of this creature's loins and the power in the muscles of its belly.
God described to Job a beast whose tail sways like a cedar, its thigh sinews tightly knit.
God told Job this beast's bones are tubes of bronze and its limbs are like rods of iron.
God told Job this creature is the foremost of His works, and only its Maker can draw the sword against it.
In God's words to Job, this beast lies under the lotus plants, hidden among the reeds of the marsh.
God told Job this creature stays unafraid and secure even when the Jordan surges up to its mouth.
On the night He was betrayed, Jesus prayed this word, followed by 'Father,' asking God to take the cup from Him.
In Gethsemane, Jesus called God by this word before saying all things were possible for Him.
After Jesus called God this, He prayed, "Yet not what I will, but what You will."
Fallen to the ground in Gethsemane, Jesus prayed that the hour might pass, calling God this.
Paul told the Romans that believers, given a spirit of adoption, cry out this word and then 'Father!'
Writing to Rome, Paul said those freed from a spirit that returns them to fear cry out this word.
Paul told the Galatians that the Spirit of God's Son in their hearts cries this word, then 'Father!'
The angel of the LORD found this man threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding it from the Midianites.
Called to save Israel, he said his clan was the weakest in Manasseh and he was the youngest son.
Asking God for a sign before battle, he wrung a bowlful of dew from a fleece one morning.
God told this leader to keep only the three hundred men who lapped water and send the rest home.
Near the Midianite camp at night, he overheard a man telling of a dream about a tumbling barley loaf.
His men broke jars, held torches and blew horns, shouting of a sword for the LORD and for him.
After Midian was defeated, Israel asked him to rule over them, but he said the LORD would rule them.
Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and this covered all the land of Egypt for three days.
While Jesus hung on the cross, this came over all the land from the sixth hour until the ninth.
At Sinai the people stood at a distance as Moses drew near to the thick cover of this, where God was.
As the sun was setting, Abram fell into a deep sleep, and great terror and this overwhelmed him.
In Jesus' parable of the talents, the worthless servant is thrown into the outer part of this.
When Paul rebuked the sorcerer Elymas, mist and this came over him, and he groped about.
When the fifth angel poured his bowl on the beast's throne, its kingdom was plunged into this.
After her father and mother died, her cousin Mordecai raised her as his own daughter.
The king loved her more than all the other women and crowned her queen in place of Vashti.
Taken to the palace at Susa, she kept her people and lineage secret because Mordecai told her to.
Seeing this queen standing in his court, the king held out his gold scepter, and she touched its tip.
Dining with the king, she exposed Haman as the wicked adversary and enemy.
Distressed that Mordecai wore sackcloth, this queen sent him clothes, but he would not accept them.
As daughter of Abihail, she wrote with Mordecai the Jew to confirm a second letter about Purim.
When the Israelites were numbered, each man paid the LORD a ransom so no plague would come.
In the wilderness, Moses was told to list every man of Israel by clan and family, name by name.
God told Moses not to number the tribe of Levi in this along with the other Israelites.
God said all twenty or older counted in this would fall in the wilderness for grumbling.
Satan rose up against Israel and stirred King David to take this of Israel.
Joab son of Zeruiah began this count but did not finish, and wrath came upon Israel.
Gamaliel told the Sanhedrin that Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of this and drew people after him.
Gideon told God this thing he would set out was made of wool.
Gideon asked God to let dew fall only on this, while all the ground stayed dry.
Gideon said that if this alone got wet, he would know God would save Israel by his hand.
Rising the next morning, Gideon squeezed this and wrung out a bowlful of water.
Gideon begged God not to be angry with him and asked for one more test with this.
God answered Gideon's second request about this on that very same night.
Job said a poor man's heart blessed him for warming him with this from Job's sheep.
